75747.q: What does a saw have so that it can cut wood?
75747.e: The saw blade has lots of small, sharp teeth. As it moves back and forth, they remove the wood bit by bit.
75747.m: A saw cuts with its teeth.

75748.q: What is the fine wood powder called that is made when sawing?
75748.e: The teeth of the saw tear out tiny bits of wood. These fall down as fine sawdust.

75749.q: What do you use to hold the wood firmly while sawing?
75749.e: The wood must be held tightly while sawing, for example with a clamp or in a vice. Otherwise it slips and you can hurt yourself.
75749.m: When sawing, the wood must be clamped tight.

75750.q: Which saw can you use to cut fine curves out of thin wood?
75750.e: A fretsaw has a very thin blade. You can use it to cut curves and shapes out of thin plywood.
75750.m: You cut fine curves with a fretsaw.

75752.q: Why should you wear safety goggles when sawing?
a: So that no bits of wood fly into your eyes
So that the wood looks nicer
So that the saw is quieter
75752.e: When sawing, small bits of wood can fly around. Safety goggles protect your eyes from them.
75752.m: Safety goggles protect your eyes in the workshop.

75753.q: What do you draw on the wood before you saw?
75753.e: With a pencil and ruler you mark exactly where to saw. This makes the cut straight and in the right place.
75753.m: Before sawing, you mark the line.

75754.q: What do you usually need a hammer for?
75754.e: You use a hammer to knock nails into wood. While doing so, you take good care of your fingers.
75754.m: You knock in nails with a hammer.

75755.q: What are the two main parts of a hammer?
75755.e: A hammer has a heavy metal head and a handle to hold it by. The handle is often made of wood.
75755.m: A hammer has a head and a handle.

75756.q: What is the split, curved part of a claw hammer for?
75756.e: On a claw hammer, one side of the head is split. You can use it to grip a bent nail and pull it out.
75756.m: You pull out nails with the claw.

75757.q: Which hammer has a head made of rubber or wood so that it does not scratch anything?
75757.e: A soft hammer made of wood or rubber knocks parts together without making dents. You need it, for example, when fitting wooden parts together.
75757.m: A rubber mallet leaves no dents.

75758.q: What are nails usually made of?
75758.e: Nails are usually made of steel, which is a metal. That is why they are hard enough to go into wood.
75758.m: Nails are usually made of metal.

75759.q: What is the wide, flat end of a nail that you hit called?
75759.e: A nail has a flat head at the top and a point at the bottom. You hit the head with the hammer.
75759.m: You hit the head of the nail with the hammer.

75760.q: How do you start knocking in a nail?
a: Hold the nail with two fingers and tap lightly
Hold the nail with two fingers and hit hard straight away
Let go of the nail and hit hard straight away
Hold the nail in your fist and hit hard
75760.e: At first you hold the nail between your thumb and index finger and tap very lightly. As soon as it is firmly in, you take your fingers away and hit harder.
75760.m: First tap lightly, then hit harder.

75761.q: What often happens if you knock a nail in too close to the edge of a plank?
75761.e: The nail pushes the wood fibres apart. If there is too little wood at the edge, the plank splits.
75761.m: Do not knock nails in too close to the edge.

75762.q: What is the small hole in a sewing needle called, through which you thread the cotton?
75762.e: A sewing needle has a point at one end and a small hole at the other. This hole is called the eye.
75762.m: The thread goes through the eye of the needle.

75763.q: What protects your finger from the needle when sewing by hand?
75763.e: You put the thimble on your middle finger. With it you can push the needle through the fabric without pricking yourself.
75763.m: A thimble protects your finger when sewing.

75764.q: What do you put at the end of the thread so that it does not slip through the fabric?
75764.e: A knot at the end of the thread is thicker than the hole in the fabric. That way the thread stays caught at the first stitch.
75764.m: A knot holds the thread in the fabric.

75765.q: What is the line called where two pieces of fabric are sewn together?
75765.e: Where two pieces of fabric are joined with stitches, a seam is formed. On clothes you can see seams at the sides, for example.
75765.m: A seam joins two pieces of fabric.

75766.q: What is the simple stitch called where the needle keeps going up and down through the fabric?
75766.e: With running stitch, you stitch up and down at equal distances. This makes a dashed line.
75766.m: Running stitch is a simple up-and-down stitch.

75767.q: In which stitch do two slanting stitches together form an X?
75767.e: In cross stitch, you first sew a slanting stitch and then cross it with a second one. This way pictures are made from lots of little Xs.

75768.q: Which machine lets you sew faster than by hand?
75768.e: A sewing machine moves the needle up and down very fast. This makes long, even seams in a short time.

75769.q: What do you use to fix pieces of fabric together before sewing?
75769.e: Pins often have a small head. You use them to hold the pieces of fabric in place so that they do not slip while sewing.
75769.m: Pins hold fabric together before sewing.

75770.q: What do you need buttons on clothes for?
75770.e: A button is pushed through a small slit in the fabric. This keeps a shirt or jacket closed, for example.

75771.q: What is the slit in the fabric that you push the button through called?
75771.e: A buttonhole is a narrow slit with a sewn edge. The button fits exactly through it.
75771.m: The button goes in the buttonhole.

75772.q: How many holes do many flat buttons have?
75772.e: Many flat buttons have two or four holes. You sew the button onto the fabric through these holes.
75772.m: Many buttons have two or four holes.

75773.q: What do you need to sew a button back on?
75773.e: You thread a needle and sew through the holes of the button into the fabric. At the end you fasten off the thread well.
75773.m: You sew on a button with needle and thread.

75774.q: What is a button called that has two parts and is pressed shut with a click?
75774.e: A press stud has a top part and a bottom part. When you press them together, they snap into place with a click.
75774.m: A press stud closes with a click.

75775.q: What can buttons be made of, for example?
75775.e: Buttons come in many materials. They are often made of plastic, metal, wood or horn.

75776.q: Which fastening is often used on jackets instead of buttons and has lots of little teeth?
75776.e: In a zip, lots of little teeth lock into each other. You open and close it quickly with the slider.
75776.m: A zip has lots of little teeth.

75777.q: How many strands do you use to make a simple plait?
75777.e: For a simple plait, you divide hair or threads into three strands. Then you take turns laying the left and the right strand over the middle one.
75777.m: A simple plait has three strands.

75778.q: Which Swiss Sunday bread is plaited from strands of dough?
75778.e: In Switzerland, people often eat butter Zopf for breakfast on Sundays. The dough is plaited before baking.
75778.m: The Sunday Zopf is plaited from dough.

75779.q: What material are baskets often woven from?
75779.e: Willow rods are long and bendy. That is why they are easy to weave into strong baskets.
75779.m: Baskets are often woven from willow rods.

75780.q: What do you do with the strands when plaiting?
a: You lay them over each other in turn
75780.e: When plaiting, you cross several strands over each other in turn. This way they hold together without glue.
75780.m: When plaiting, the strands cross over each other in turn.

75781.q: What can you weave from strips of paper?
75781.e: You cut paper into strips and weave them over and under each other. This makes a colourful paper mat.
75781.m: You can weave a mat from paper strips.

75782.q: Which device is used to weave fabric?
75782.e: Lots of threads are stretched on a loom. You pass a crosswise thread over and under them again and again.
75782.m: Fabric is woven on a loom.

75783.q: What are the threads stretched lengthways in weaving called?
75783.e: The warp threads are first stretched tightly lengthways. The crosswise thread that is passed through them is called the weft.
75783.m: In weaving, the warp threads run lengthways.

75784.q: What do you need the weaving comb for when weaving?
a: To push the crosswise threads tightly together
75784.e: After each row, you press the new crosswise thread against the previous rows with the weaving comb. This makes the fabric dense and firm.
75784.m: The weaving comb pushes the rows tightly together.

75785.q: What is the firm edge at the side of a woven fabric that does not fray called?
75785.e: At the side, the crosswise thread turns and runs back. This creates a firm edge, the selvedge, which does not fray.
75785.m: The selvedge is the firm edge of a woven fabric.

75786.q: What do you use to pass the thread through when weaving on a small weaving frame?
a: A weaving needle or a shuttle
75786.e: The crosswise thread is wound onto a shuttle or threaded into a large weaving needle. This lets you pass it easily through the stretched threads.
75786.m: The shuttle carries the thread when weaving.

75787.q: What can you weave on a small weaving frame at school?
75787.e: A small weaving frame produces a small, flat piece of fabric. You can make it into a coaster or a doll's rug, for example.
75787.m: A weaving frame makes a small piece of fabric.

75788.q: Which part of the cotton plant are cotton fibres obtained from?
75788.e: Cotton fibres grow as fine hairs on the seeds inside the seed pod. When the pod bursts open, the white fibre puffs out.
75788.m: Cotton is made of the seed hairs of the cotton plant.

75789.q: Why are towels often made of cotton?
a: It soaks up a lot of water.
It builds up a lot of static.
75789.e: Cotton is very absorbent and can take up a lot of moisture. That is why cotton towels dry you well.
75789.m: Cotton is absorbent, so it is good for towels.

75790.q: Which protein is the main component of sheep's wool?
75790.e: Wool is animal hair and, like our hair and nails, is made mainly of the protein keratin.
75790.m: Sheep's wool is made mainly of the protein keratin.

75791.q: Why can a woollen jumper felt in water that is too hot with lots of rubbing?
a: The fibres have scales that hook together.
75791.e: Wool hairs have a layer of scales. With warmth, moisture and movement, the scales hook together and the fabric becomes dense and smaller.
75791.m: Wool felts because the scales of the hairs hook into each other.

75792.q: Which leaves does the silkworm caterpillar feed on?
75792.e: The caterpillar of the silk moth eats the leaves of the mulberry tree. Then it spins itself into a cocoon made of one long silk thread.

75793.q: Which natural fibre is a very long continuous thread (filament)?
75793.e: The silkworm's cocoon is made of a single thread several hundred metres long. Other natural fibres are short fibres that have to be spun into yarn.
75793.m: Silk is the only natural fibre that comes as a continuous thread.

75794.q: Which plant is the fibre for linen obtained from?
75794.e: Linen is made from the stem fibres of flax. Linen fabrics are strong and feel cool.

75795.q: What raw material is polyester mainly made from?
75795.e: Polyester is a synthetic fibre made of plastic. The plastic is usually made from crude oil.
75795.m: Polyester is a synthetic fibre made from crude oil.

75796.q: What happens to a polyester fibre in a burn test?
a: It melts into a hard bead.
It burns to soft, grey ash.
It does not burn at all.
75796.e: Polyester is a plastic and melts in the flame. Afterwards a hard ball is left that you cannot crush.
75796.m: Synthetic fibres melt into hard beads in a burn test.

75797.q: In weaving, what is the opening between the raised and the lowered warp threads called?
75797.e: Raising some of the warp threads creates a gap. The crosswise thread is passed through this shed.
75797.m: In weaving, the crosswise thread runs through the shed.

75798.q: What is the thread called that is passed crosswise through the stretched threads in weaving?
75798.e: The weft thread is shot crosswise between the lengthways threads. Together the two sets of threads form the fabric.
75798.m: The crosswise thread in weaving is called the weft.

75799.q: Which tool is used to pass the crosswise thread through the warp on a loom?
75799.e: The shuttle carries a small bobbin with the thread. It is pushed from one side to the other through the opened warp threads.
75799.m: The shuttle carries the crosswise thread through the warp.

75800.q: Which part of the loom presses the new crosswise thread firmly against the finished fabric?
75800.e: The reed is a comb-like part that the warp threads run through. You use it to beat each new weft thread into place so that the fabric is dense.
75800.m: The reed beats each weft thread into place.

75801.q: In weaving, what are the lengthways threads called that are stretched tight first?
75801.e: First you stretch the lengthways threads, the warp. Then the crosswise thread, the weft, is passed through again and again.
75801.m: The stretched lengthways threads in weaving are called the warp.

75802.q: In which weave does the crosswise thread always go alternately over one and under one lengthways thread?
75802.e: Plain weave is the simplest and strongest kind of weave. The threads cross at every change.
75802.m: In plain weave, the thread goes over one and under one in turn.

75803.q: Which weave can you recognise by diagonal lines in the fabric, for example in jeans?
75803.e: In twill weave, the crossing points shift by one thread from row to row. This creates a diagonal ridge that is typical of denim.
75803.m: You can recognise twill weave by its diagonal lines.

75804.q: What controlled the patterns on the Jacquard loom around 1805?
75804.e: Joseph-Marie Jacquard from Lyon controlled his loom with punched cards. These cards are seen as early forerunners of computer programming.
75804.m: The Jacquard loom is controlled by punched cards.

75805.q: What is the knitting pattern called where you knit the right-side rows and purl the wrong-side rows?
75805.e: This makes a smooth surface with small V-shaped stitches on the front. On the back you only see purl stitches.
75805.m: Stocking stitch comes from knit rows on the front and purl rows on the back.

75806.q: What are the two basic stitches in knitting?
75806.e: Almost all knitting patterns are made of knit and purl stitches. A knit stitch looks like a purl stitch on the back.
75806.m: The basic stitches in knitting are knit and purl.

75807.q: What is the knitting pattern called where you knit every row with knit stitches only?
75807.e: If you knit only knit stitches there and back, horizontal ridges appear on both sides. This pattern is called garter stitch.
75807.m: Garter stitch comes from knitting every row.

75808.q: What are socks traditionally knitted in the round with?
75808.e: A set of double-pointed needles usually has five short needles with points at both ends. The stitches are spread over four needles and you knit with the fifth.
75808.m: Socks are knitted in the round with double-pointed needles.

75809.q: What do you call finishing a piece of knitting so that the stitches do not come undone?
75809.e: When casting off, you pull each stitch over the next one until only one loop is left. Then the yarn is pulled through and sewn in.
75809.m: At the end, a piece of knitting is cast off.

75810.q: Why is a knitted fabric usually stretchier than a woven fabric?
a: It is made of loops hooked into each other.
It is made only of synthetic fibres.
75810.e: Stitches are loops that can change shape and shift. In a woven fabric, straight threads cross and hardly give at all.
75810.m: Knitting is stretchy because it is made of loops.

75811.q: What do you usually start a piece of crochet with?
75811.e: First you crochet a chain of chain stitches as wide as you want. Then you crochet the first row into this chain.
75811.m: A piece of crochet usually starts with a foundation chain.

75812.q: Which crochet stitch starts by wrapping the yarn once around the hook before inserting it?
75812.e: For a treble, you first wrap the yarn over the hook and then insert it. This makes the stitch taller than a double crochet.
75812.m: A treble starts with a yarn over.

75813.q: How many hooks do you need for crocheting?
75813.e: When crocheting, you work with a single hook. There is only ever one loop left on the hook.
75813.m: You only need one hook for crocheting.

75814.q: Where does the bottom thread on a sewing machine come from?
a: From the bobbin under the needle plate
From the reel of thread at the top
75814.e: The bottom thread is wound onto a small bobbin that sits in the hook under the needle plate. The top thread comes from the reel of thread.
75814.m: The bottom thread comes from the bobbin under the needle plate.

75815.q: What is the basic stitch of a household sewing machine called, where the top and bottom threads loop around each other?
75815.e: In lockstitch, the bottom thread catches the loop of the top thread. The link lies in the middle of the fabric and the seam looks the same on both sides.
75815.m: A sewing machine sews with lockstitch.

75816.q: Which sewing machine stitch is used to finish fabric edges so that they do not fray?
75816.e: Zigzag stitch wraps around the cut edge and holds the threads in place. This stops the fabric fraying.
75816.m: Zigzag stitch is used to finish fabric edges.

75817.q: Which part of the sewing machine moves the fabric along stitch by stitch while sewing?
75817.e: The feed dogs are toothed bars under the presser foot. They move and pull the fabric towards the back.
75817.m: The feed dogs move the fabric along under the presser foot.

75818.q: Where is the eye of a sewing machine needle?
a: At the top by the shank
In the middle of the needle
75818.e: Unlike a hand sewing needle, the eye is just above the point. This allows the top thread to be taken under the fabric.
75818.m: On a sewing machine needle, the eye is near the point.

75819.q: Why do you sew a few stitches backwards at the start and end of a seam?
a: So that the seam does not come undone
So that the needle cools down
75819.e: Sewing backwards locks the threads in place. That way the seam cannot open while the clothes are being worn.
75819.m: Sewing backwards secures the start and end of a seam.

75820.q: Loops of the top thread form on the underside of the fabric. What is usually the cause?
a: The top thread tension is too loose.
75820.e: If the top thread is not tight enough, the bottom thread pulls it down. Often the top thread is also threaded incorrectly.
75820.m: Loops underneath point to a top thread that is too loose.

75821.q: In which century were the first usable sewing machines invented?
75821.e: Around 1830, the Frenchman Barthélemy Thimonnier received a patent for a sewing machine. During the 19th century the machines found their way into factories and homes.
75821.m: The sewing machine was invented in the 19th century.

75822.q: What does the long arrow on a pattern piece show?
75822.e: The arrow must lie parallel to the edge of the fabric along which the lengthways threads run. Then the garment hangs straight and does not twist.
75822.m: The arrow on a pattern piece shows the grain line.

75823.q: What do you call the extra edge of fabric outside the stitching line?
75823.e: The seam allowance is added when cutting out so that you can sew the fabric together. It is often 1 to 1.5 cm wide.
75823.m: Outside the stitching line you need a seam allowance.

75824.q: When cutting out, what does the instruction “place on fold” mean?
a: The piece is placed against the folded edge of the fabric.
The fabric is torn instead of cut.
The piece is placed at a slant.
75824.e: You fold the fabric and place the centre line of the pattern piece on the fold. This creates a symmetrical piece twice as wide with no seam in the middle.
75824.m: A piece cut on the fold is cut along the folded edge.

75825.q: What is a tapering seam called that shapes a garment to the body?
75825.e: A dart takes away fabric in a point. This creates a curve, for example at the waist.
75825.m: Darts shape fabric to the body.

75826.q: What are notches on a sewing pattern for?
75826.e: Notches are small marks on the edges. When the marks on two pieces meet, the pieces are in the right position.
75826.m: Notches show which points belong together.

75827.q: Which tool is used to transfer the lines of a sewing pattern onto fabric with carbon paper?
75827.e: A tracing wheel has a small jagged wheel. You run it along the lines, and the dressmaker's carbon paper presses the line onto the fabric.
75827.m: A tracing wheel transfers pattern lines.

75828.q: Which body measurement do you take at the narrowest part of the torso?
75828.e: The waist is the narrowest point between the ribcage and the hips. You measure it loosely all the way round with a tape measure.
75828.m: You measure the waist at the narrowest part of the torso.

75829.q: What is the turned-up and sewn-down bottom edge of trousers or a skirt called?
75829.e: When hemming, the edge of the fabric is folded over and sewn down. This stops it fraying and gets the length right.
75829.m: The bottom edge of a garment is called the hem.

75830.q: Which of these kinds of wood is a softwood from a conifer?
75830.e: The spruce has needles and cones. Beech, oak and maple are broadleaf trees.

75831.q: Which tree species is the most common in Swiss forests?
75831.e: According to the Swiss National Forest Inventory, the spruce is the most common tree species in Switzerland. Its wood is widely used as building timber.
75831.m: The spruce is the most common tree in Switzerland.

75832.q: What can you tell from the growth rings of a tree trunk?
75832.e: In our climate, a tree forms a light and a dark layer of wood every year. If you count these rings, you know its age.
75832.m: Each growth ring stands for one year of growth.

75833.q: Which very light wood is often used for making models?
75833.e: Balsa wood comes from Central and South America and is one of the lightest timbers. You can even cut it with a knife.
75833.m: Balsa wood is very light and is used for model making.

75834.q: Which conifer wood from the Alps is known for its scent and is often used for living rooms and beds?
75834.e: The Swiss stone pine, also called arolla pine, grows in the Alps up to the tree line. Its wood has a strong scent and is traditionally used in the Engadine for panelled stone pine rooms.
75834.m: Swiss stone pine smells good and is often used for panelled rooms.

75835.q: What is the wood material made of several thin layers of wood glued crosswise called?
75835.e: In plywood, the wood fibres of each layer run across those of the next. This means it hardly warps and is very strong.
75835.m: Plywood is made of layers of wood glued crosswise.

75836.q: Which soft, even wood is especially good for carving?
75836.e: Lime wood is soft, has fine fibres and hardly splinters. Many wooden figures and nativity figures are carved from lime.
75836.m: Lime wood is ideal for carving.

75837.q: How do you fit a blade into a fretsaw?
a: Teeth pointing down towards the handle
Teeth pointing up towards the tip
75837.e: A fretsaw cuts on the downward stroke. That is why the teeth must point down towards the handle.
75837.m: On a fretsaw, the teeth point towards the handle.

75838.q: What is the best thing to rest the workpiece on when using a fretsaw?
a: A fretsaw table with a V-shaped cut-out
75838.e: The small table is screwed onto the workbench. In the V-shaped cut-out you can hold the wood safely and saw.
75838.m: When using a fretsaw, the wood rests on a fretsaw table.

75839.q: How do you move the fretsaw when sawing a curve?
a: Straight up and down, turning the wood
At a slant and fast forwards
75839.e: You hold the saw upright and move it evenly up and down. On curves you slowly turn the workpiece, not the saw.
75839.m: On curves, you turn the wood when using a fretsaw.

75840.q: What do you use a file for in the workshop?
75840.e: A file has lots of small cutting edges on its surface. You use it to remove material and make edges smooth.
75840.m: You smooth and shape edges with a file.

75841.q: In which direction does a file work?
75841.e: The teeth of the file point forwards. That is why you press on the forward stroke and pull the file back without pressure.
75841.m: A file cuts on the forward stroke.

75842.q: Which file-like tool with separate coarse teeth is used for wood?
75842.e: A rasp removes a lot of material at once. Afterwards you smooth the surface with a file and sandpaper.

75843.q: How can you recognise a wood drill bit?
75843.e: A wood drill bit has a small point in the middle. It stops the bit slipping when you start drilling.
75843.m: A wood drill bit has a centre point.

75844.q: How do you set the speed of the drill for a large drill bit?
75844.e: At the edge of a large drill bit, the speed is already high at only a few turns. Too high a speed makes the bit hot and blunt.
75844.m: Large drill bits need a low speed.

75845.q: Which tool makes a cone-shaped recess so that a screw head sits flush?
75845.e: A countersink widens the edge of a drilled hole into a cone shape. A countersunk head then fits exactly and does not stick out.
75845.m: A countersink lets screw heads sit flush.

75846.q: Why do you make a small dent with a centre punch before drilling into metal?
a: So that the drill does not slip
So that the metal becomes softer
So that it is less noisy
So that the metal does not rust
75846.e: The dent guides the tip of the drill to exactly the right spot. Without centre punching, the drill would wander on the smooth surface.
75846.m: Centre punching stops the drill slipping on metal.

75847.q: What do you use to mark lines on metal?
75847.e: A scriber has a hard point and scratches a fine, clearly visible line into the surface. A pencil would not be accurate enough on metal.
75847.m: Lines on metal are marked with a scriber.

75848.q: Which saw is used in the workshop to cut through a metal pipe?
75848.e: A hacksaw has a finely toothed, hardened blade in a frame. It is made for hard materials.
75848.m: Metal is cut with a hacksaw.

75849.q: What is removing sharp edges after sawing metal called?
75849.e: Sawing leaves sharp burrs on the edge. You remove them with a file or deburring tool so that you do not cut yourself.

75850.q: What do you put between the vice and a delicate workpiece so that it does not get marked?
75850.e: The jaws of a vice are ridged and leave marks. Soft jaws made of aluminium, plastic or wood protect the workpiece.
75850.m: Soft jaws stop marks in the vice.

75851.q: What do you do when soldering in electronics?
a: You join metal parts with melted metal
You stick parts together with glue
You weld plastic with a flame
75851.e: The hot soldering iron melts the solder, which is made mainly of tin. It flows around the components and, once it cools, joins them firmly and conductively.
75851.m: When soldering, melted solder joins the metal parts.

75852.q: Which metals is the alloy brass made of?
75852.e: Brass is a golden-yellow alloy of copper and zinc. It is used for brass instruments and door handles, for example.
75852.m: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

75853.q: Which metal is used for cables because it conducts electricity very well?
75853.e: After silver, copper conducts electricity best and is much cheaper. That is why most cable wires are made of copper.
75853.m: Electric cables are usually made of copper.

75854.q: Which of these joints can be undone again without destroying parts?
75854.e: A screw can be unscrewed and put back in. Rivets, glue and welds have to be destroyed to separate the parts.

75855.q: Which rivet can you fit if you can only reach the workpiece from one side?
75855.e: A blind rivet, also called a pop rivet, is set from one side with a rivet gun. The mandrel pulls the rivet together on the back.
75855.m: Blind rivets are set from one side.

75856.q: Which glue is usually used at school for wood joints?
75856.e: PVA glue is a water-based wood glue. It is white when you apply it and becomes almost clear as it dries.
75856.m: Wood is usually glued with PVA glue.

75857.q: What do you use to press freshly glued pieces of wood together until the glue is dry?
75857.e: Glue holds best when the parts are pressed firmly together. Clamps keep up the pressure until the glue has set.

75858.q: Why do you drill a pilot hole before driving a screw into hard wood near the edge?
a: So that the wood does not split
So that the screw gets longer
So that the glue holds better
75858.e: A screw pushes the wood fibres apart. A small pilot hole stops the wood splitting at the edge.
75858.m: Drilling a pilot hole stops wood splitting.

75859.q: What is the spiral groove on a screw called?
75859.e: As you turn the screw, the thread pulls it into the material and holds it tight. A nail has no thread.
75859.m: A screw holds thanks to its thread.

75860.q: What do you put into a drilled hole in a concrete wall so that a screw will hold in it?
75860.e: The plastic wall plug spreads out when the screw is turned in. This way it wedges itself tightly in the hole.
75860.m: In concrete, a screw needs a wall plug.

75861.q: What is a screw head with a six-pointed star-shaped recess usually called?
75861.e: With Torx, the screwdriver grips a star with six rounded points. It slips less easily than a slot.
75861.m: A Torx screw head has a six-pointed star.

75862.q: What is needed for a lamp to light up in an electric circuit?
a: Just one wire to the positive terminal
75862.e: Current only flows if there is an unbroken path from one terminal of the battery through the lamp to the other terminal. Any gap stops the current.
75862.m: Current only flows in a closed circuit.

75863.q: Two lamps are connected in series. What happens if one lamp breaks?
a: The other lamp goes out too.
75863.e: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current. If one lamp fails, the whole circuit is broken.
75863.m: In a series circuit, a broken lamp breaks the whole circuit.

75864.q: In which circuit do the other lamps stay on if one lamp fails?
75864.e: In a parallel circuit, each lamp has its own path for the current. That is why the lights in a flat are also connected in parallel.
75864.m: Lamps connected in parallel work independently of each other.

75865.q: Which of these objects conducts electricity?
75865.e: Metals are good electrical conductors. Rubber, dry wood and plastic are insulators.
75865.m: Metals conduct electricity; plastic and rubber insulate.

75866.q: Which leg of an LED is normally connected to the positive terminal?
75866.e: The longer leg is the anode and goes to positive. An LED only lights up if it is connected the right way round.
75866.m: The longer leg of the LED goes to the positive terminal.

75867.q: Why does an LED on a 9-volt battery need a series resistor?
75867.e: Without a resistor, too much current would flow through the LED and it would be destroyed. The series resistor limits the current to a safe level.
75867.m: A series resistor protects the LED from too much current.

75868.q: What does a switch do in the “off” position?
a: It connects plus and minus directly.
75868.e: In the “off” position, a switch opens a gap in the circuit. Then no more current can flow.
75868.m: An open switch breaks the circuit.

75869.q: What is it called when the positive and negative terminals of a battery are connected directly with a wire?
75869.e: In a short circuit, a lot of current flows without anything using it. The wire and the battery can get hot.
75869.m: A short circuit happens when plus and minus are connected directly.

75870.q: What voltage does a typical flat battery often used in school lessons have?
75870.e: A flat battery contains three cells of 1.5 volts each connected in series. Together that makes 3 times 1.5 V, which is 4.5 V.
75870.m: A flat battery has a voltage of 4.5 volts.

75871.q: What should you always wear when drilling and sanding to protect your eyes?
75871.e: When drilling and sanding, shavings and dust fly off. Safety goggles prevent eye injuries.
75871.m: Safety goggles protect your eyes when drilling and sanding.

75872.q: What must you do with long hair before working at a pillar drill?
a: Nothing, it does not get in the way
75872.e: Loose hair can be caught and wound up by the turning drill spindle. That can lead to serious injuries.
75872.m: Long hair is tied back when using machines.

75873.q: Why do you not wear gloves at a pillar drill?
a: They can get caught by the drill.
They make your hands too warm.
75873.e: A glove can get caught on the turning drill and pull your hand in. That is why gloves are banned at rotating machines.
75873.m: Do not wear gloves at rotating machines.

75874.q: How do you hold a small workpiece when drilling at a pillar drill?
75874.e: The drill can catch and spin the workpiece around. Clamped in a machine vice, it stays safely in place.
75874.m: When drilling, the workpiece is always clamped.

75875.q: Which Swiss institution insures employees against accidents and publishes rules on accident prevention?
75875.e: Suva is the Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund, based in Lucerne. It also gives information on working safely in workshops.
75875.m: Suva works for accident prevention in Switzerland.

75876.q: In which direction do you cut with a craft knife or carving knife?
75876.e: If the knife slips, it slides away from your body into empty space. The holding hand stays behind the blade.
75876.m: Always cut away from your body.

75877.q: What do you do if a machine's cable is damaged?
a: Unplug it, do not use it and report it
Wrap it in tape and keep working
75877.e: A damaged cable can cause an electric shock. Only a specialist may repair it.
75877.m: Report damaged cables at once and do not use the machine.

75878.q: Where do you put a hot soldering iron during a break in your work?
75878.e: The tip of a soldering iron is several hundred degrees hot. In the stand, nobody can get burnt and nothing catches fire.
75878.m: A hot soldering iron always goes in its stand.

a: Making a product of higher value from waste
Getting rid of waste at the incineration plant
75879.e: In upcycling, an old object is turned into something new and more valuable. The material is not broken down first.
75879.m: Upcycling turns waste into something more valuable.

75880.q: What is it called when a waste material is turned into a product of lower quality?
75880.e: In downcycling, a material loses quality, for example when office paper becomes cardboard or toilet paper. Afterwards it often cannot be used in the same way again.
75880.m: Downcycling means a material loses value.

a: Sewing a bag from an old pair of jeans
Taking a PET bottle to a collection point
Buying a new pair of jeans
75881.e: The jeans are turned directly into a new, useful object. Handing in PET or paper is part of recycling.
75881.m: A bag made from old jeans is an example of upcycling.

75882.q: Since 1993, which used material has the Zurich company Freitag made bags from?
75882.e: In 1993, the brothers Markus and Daniel Freitag sewed a first bike courier bag from old lorry tarpaulins. It is a well-known Swiss example of upcycling.
75882.m: Freitag bags are made from old lorry tarpaulins.

75883.q: Why is upcycling good for the environment?
a: It saves raw materials and energy.
75883.e: An existing object is used again instead of being thrown away. This means fewer new materials have to be made.
75883.m: Upcycling saves raw materials and energy.

75884.q: What comes first in the waste hierarchy?
75884.e: It is best if no waste is produced at all. Only after that come reusing, recycling and finally burning or landfill.
